[p. 423] **The Sura of Mankind (Surat al-Nas).** Its purpose is seeking refuge in the true God from the inner evil of creation. Its name points to this, because man is inclined toward evil, and most of his evil is through deceit and trickery. A better explanation is that it is for seeking refuge from the inner evil that is familiar to a person and that he finds comfort in, since whispering (al-waswasa) only occurs through what one desires. "Mankind" (al-nas) is derived from intimacy (al-uns), for its origin is *unas*. It also means the agitation of the inner self, to which the derivation from *al-nawS* (swaying, agitation) points. Thus the name corresponds to what it names. The purpose of this sura is dependent on the purpose of al-Fatiha, which is watchfulness (al-muraqaba). This purpose encompasses all the sciences of the Qur'an, which are the befriending of God and the enmity toward Satan, with the excellence of the conclusion and the summation of the order. Just as al-Fatiha encompasses this, because it is the excellence of the opening and the observance of majesty and beauty, the last is connected to the first with the connection of cause to effect, proof to what is proven, and example to what is exemplified. God is the one asked to facilitate the request and realize the hoped-for, for He is the Generous, possessor of bounty, by Him one seeks help and upon Him one relies: "In the name of God" (bismillah), who encompasses [in knowledge] every (p. 424) inner thing as He encompasses every outer thing; "the Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), whose blessing has embraced every present and absent thing; "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who has singled out His friends with the completion of blessing upon them in all their affairs, the first of them, the middle and the last.

* *

When the Sura of the Daybreak (Surat al-Falaq) came for seeking refuge from the evil of what He created, from all the bodily harms and others that are general to man and other than man, that is the totality of evil existing in all the realms and times. Then specification occurred within it with particular evils: from the wrongdoer, the sorcerer, and the envier. So seeking refuge in it was general to the external calamities that return to the injustice of others, and to the internal faults that return to the injustice of the self, but it is more apparent in calamities. It concluded with envy, so it is known that envy is the most harmful of calamities, and the origin of enmity between jinn and humans is envy. The Sura of Mankind came including seeking refuge from a particular evil, which is whispering. It is more specific than the general envier, and it returns to the inner faults attached to human souls, all of which originate in whispering, and it is the cause of all sins and disobediences. It is more likely and more harmful from the jinn. All evil returns to calamities and faults. So this sura, like al-Falaq, comprises seeking refuge, one sought refuge in, one sought refuge from, and a command to bring this about. The command is ﴿Say﴾, the seeking refuge is ﴿I seek refuge﴾, and the one sought refuge in is (p. 425) God, glorified and exalted. But since the attribute of lordship is among the attributes of His perfection, glorified be He, it is most fitting for protection, aid, care, creation, governance, nurturing and reform, which include complete power, vast mercy, comprehensive beneficence, and perfect knowledge. God, exalted, said: ﴿With the Lord of mankind﴾ [meaning: I hold fast to Him], that is, I ask Him to be my protector from the enemy, from causing me to fall into destruction. Al-Malawi said: The Lord (al-Rabb) is the one who possesses dominion over the slave, brings goodness from the heavens and the earth and preserves it, repels evils and removes them, moves from deficiency to perfection, and manages generally, returning with preservation and completion upon the one nurtured. The attribution is specified to those who are shaken and agitated in bodies and religions, among mankind and jinn, because of the particularity of what one seeks refuge from, which is harms that befall rational souls and are specific to them, unlike what is in al-Falaq, which is bodily harms that are general to man and others.

Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: The reason it comes after its sister is that the first is general and the second is specific. Do you not see the generality of His saying ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ [al-Falaq: 2], and the vagueness of "what" (ma), and the indefiniteness of ﴿darkness when it settles﴾ [al-Falaq: 3] and ﴿an envier﴾ [al-Falaq: 5]? As for the specific, what is sought refuge from is in the Sura of Mankind, with its definition and description. So it begins with the general and then follows with the specific, to be more eloquent in achieving what the seeking of refuge intends, and more complete in the purpose. A parallel to this, in presenting the more general meaning and then following it with the more specific, in addressing the subtleties and the grand matters, is His saying, glorified and exalted: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." The meaning of "the Most Gracious" and the meaning of "the Most Merciful" are one, not in the generality of the first attribute, and that it is for emphasis. The commentators have addressed the explanation of this, and there are similar examples to this. End.

Since "Lord" (al-Rabb) and "King" (al-Malik) are close in meaning, and "Lord" is closer in meaning to kindness (al-lutf) and nurturing (al-tarbiyah), while "King" more necessarily implies subjugation (al-qahr), dominion (al-istila'), and the manifestation of justice (idhhar al-'adl), and since "Lord" may not be a king and so would not have complete authority over disposal (kamil al-tasarruf), eloquence requires placing the first (Lord) and following it with the second. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿the King of mankind﴾, indicating that He possesses complete authority over disposal, unrestricted power, and perfect sovereignty; to Him is the recourse, He is the One sought for help, the One sought for relief, the refuge, and the final return.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 114, verse 3:**

Since a king may not be a god, and divinity (*uluhiyya*, the quality of being the one worthy of worship) is a unique attribute that admits no partner at all, unlike other attributes, the matter was referred to it and made the final point of the explanation. So He said: (p. 427) ﴿The God of mankind﴾, indicating that just as He alone is their Lord and King, with no one sharing that with Him, so He alone is their God, and no one shares His divinity. This has always been the method of the Qur'an: it argues against them by their acknowledgement of His oneness in lordship (*rububiyya*) and sovereignty, concerning what they denied of His oneness in divinity and worship. Whoever is their Lord and King is deserving that they not take any other as God, nor seek refuge in anyone else. Just as one of them, when a calamity befalls him, seeks refuge in his protector from among his own kind and calls on him for help. The God is the one who manifests Himself through His subtle works, which the concept of Lord and King conveyed to the hearts of the servants, so they loved Him, felt intimate with Him, and turned to Him in all their affairs. [And He was hidden -] veiled by His greatness from being encompassed, either by Him or by any of His attributes or any aspect of His affairs. So the servants stood in awe of Him, and love summoned them to ecstatic longing (*walah*) out of yearning for meeting Him, and awe restrained them, so they grieved in fear of His expelling them from His presence. He repeated the apparent noun instead of using a pronoun, so that He would not say, for example, "their King" or "their God," in order to affirm this meaning and strengthen it by repeating their name, which indicates the intensity of distress that calls for need, with each of His names indicating perfection that calls for absolute self-sufficiency. It also indicates that He is worthy of being returned to and capable of it, to show that He is the one who disposes of them in every respect, and to show the nobility of the human being and the greater reliance that comes with greater clarification. And so that no one would think that any of these names is restricted by what is attached to it, (p. 428) since when a pronoun is repeated, what is meant by it is the very thing it refers back to. So by repetition it is indicated that each of these attributes is general, not restricted to anything at all. Included in this seeking of refuge are all the forms of seeking refuge from all aspects of nurture, all the aspects attributed to the one seeking refuge insofar as he is under the dominion of the King (with the *damm*, the vowel on the letter *mim* of *malik*), and all the aspects attributed to divinity, so that no defect may occur in any of those aspects. This treats the difference of attributes as the difference of essences, indicating the greatness of the calamity from which refuge is sought. He did not join them with the conjunction *wa* ("and"), because of what it implies of distinction, while the intent is seeking refuge in the whole of these attributes applied to one essence, so much so that they are as if they were one attribute. He placed lordship first for its generality and comprehensiveness over every one who is nurtured, equally. So no act is performed by anyone except that He created it, glorified and exalted is He, and He is the one who prompts it. He placed divinity last for its specificity, because whoever is not bound by His commands and prohibitions has removed himself from taking Him as his God, even though in reality there is no god besides Him. He placed the attribute of King in the middle, because the King is the one who disposes by command and prohibition, and His sovereignty over them follows from His creating them. So His sovereignty is part of the perfection of His lordship, and His being their true God is part of the perfection of His sovereignty. Thus His lordship entails and necessitates His sovereignty, and His sovereignty entails and necessitates His divinity. These three attributions comprise all the foundations of faith, and contain the meanings of His beautiful names, for (p. 429) the Lord is the Capable, the Creator, besides other things on which reform, mercy, and the power that is the meaning of lordship depend, of the attributes of beauty. The King is the One who commands and forbids, who bestows honor and humiliation, besides other names that return to greatness and majesty. As for the God, He is the one who comprises all the attributes of perfection and descriptions of [majesty -], so all the beautiful names are included in Him. Since He includes in Himself all the meanings of the names, the one seeking refuge is deserving of seeking it. The arrangement of these attributes has been set in the most perfect order, indicating oneness. For whoever sees the apparent and hidden blessings upon him knows that he has a Nurturer. When he rises to the deeper stages of the knowledge of Him, glorified and exalted is He, he knows that He is free of need of all, while all are in need of Him, and by His command their affairs proceed. So he knows that He is their King. Then he knows, by His being singular in the governance of them after originating them, that He is the one deserving divinity with no partner in it. The readers (*qurra'*, the transmitters of the Qur'anic recitations) agreed in this surah on dropping the alif from *malik* (verse 2), unlike in al-Fatiha as has already passed, because when the sovereignty (*mulk*) is attributed to the Day, it conveys that He alone has absolute authority over everything in it, of substance and accident, and that no one has any command alongside Him or any share in any of that. This is the meaning of *mulk* with the *damm*. As for attributing the owner (*malik*) to mankind, it entails that He is their king, so if it were read that way here the meaning would be diminished. They agreed in Surat Al 'Imran (ʿImran) on affirming the alif in the attributed word and omitting it from the word attributed to, (p. 430) because the context intends that He, glorified and exalted is He, gives sovereignty to whom He wills and withholds it from whom He wills. The *mulk* with a *kasra* on the *mim* is more fitting to this meaning. The secrets of the speech of God, glorified and exalted is He, are too great for minds to encompass. The utmost that people of knowledge can attain is to infer, from what has become apparent of them, what lies beyond, and that their outward indicates their hidden.

When he had completed the seeking of refuge (*isti'adha*) from all its aspects, whose basis is benevolence, or greatness, or subjugation, or submission and humbling oneself, he mentioned that from which refuge is sought, saying: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer﴾. *Al-waswas* is a noun with the meaning of *al-waswasa* (whispering), like *al-zilzal* with the meaning of *al-zalzala* (the quaking). The intended meaning of *al-muwaswis* (the whisperer) is that it is named by its action for emphasis, because its action is its characteristic to which it is most addicted, just as exaggeration is made about the just person by naming him "justice" (*al-adl*). Waswasa is hidden speech: the casting of meanings into the heart in secrecy and repetition, just as the word that indicates it, *wassa*, is repeated. Its origin is the sound of ornaments, self-talk, and the whispering of dogs. Its wording is doubled to match its meaning, because the whisperer repeats what he breathes into the heart [and confirms it in secrecy] so that it will be accepted. Its verbal noun is with a kasra, like *al-zilzal*, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and they were shaken with a severe shaking﴾ [al-Ahzab: 11]. Every doubled form, such as *al-zalzala* and *al-radrada*, means repetition. The whisperer from the jinn runs through the son of Adam as the blood runs, as is stated in the Sahih. He whispers the sin secretly so that it will appear more attractive. He does not cease to adorn it and to stir up the desire that calls to it, until the person commits it. When the person has committed it, he whispers to others that so-and-so [did] such-and-such, until he exposes him by it. When he is exposed, the whisperer becomes bolder regarding the like of that, because he says: "What I was fearing of the rumor has happened, so nothing will be other than what was." His evil is making the person love what his nature inclines to, until he resembles him in the vileness of nature and the darkness of soul. From this arise harms, both inherent and transitive, the most harmful of which are arrogance and self-admiration, which ruined Satan. Through them the person falls into what he has fallen into himself. From arrogance arise rancor and envy. From it there oozes *batar al-haqq* (rejecting the truth), which is not accepting it, and from it disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. [And there is *ghamas al-nas* (contempt for people)], which is looking down on them, as known from the words of Satan:

﴿I am better than him﴾ [Sad: 76]. From this arises contempt for the friends of Allah the Exalted, by abandoning honoring them, withholding their rights, transgressing against them, and wronging them. From rancor, which is great enmity, there oozes withholding good and kindness, extending the tongue and hand with every evil and harm. From envy there oozes corruption of relations among people, as indicated by:

﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], to the end of the verse, and lying and deception, as is known from:

﴿And he swore to them both, "Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisors"﴾ [al-A'raf: 21], ﴿and he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 22]. From self-admiration there oozes resentment toward decree and destiny, as indicated by:

﴿He said, "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"﴾ [al-Isra': 61]. And confronting the command with knowledge, as hinted at by: ﴿I would not have prostrated to a human whom You created from clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 33]. And using analogy (*qiyas*) against the text, as guided by: ﴿I am better than him﴾ [Sad: 76], to the end of the verse. And using judging things as good or ugly, as conveyed by: ﴿I would not have prostrated to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud, molded﴾ [al-Hijr: 33]. And humiliation, which is boldness toward violations. From this there arise transitive harms, which are striving to corrupt beliefs, morals, deeds, bodies, and provisions. Then he does not cease to make himself beloved to the person by what his nature inclines to of these vices, while agreeing with him in them, until they become firmly rooted traits for him. Then his nature becomes base, and treatment does not benefit him; rather, it only increases him in wickedness, like Iblis. Whoever has a good origin and acquires what contradicts it through an incidental cause, that is removable, like a cure, as happened to Adam, peace be upon him.

Since the Supreme King, glorified is He, has not sent down a disease except that He sent down for it a remedy, and since He had made the remedy for the whispering His remembrance, glorified and exalted is He, for it drives away Satan, illuminates the heart, and purifies it, He, glorified and exalted is He, described the action of the whisperer at the time of using the remedy, to inform that he is of severe enmity toward the human, so that caution against him and distance from him will intensify. So He said: ﴿the retreating one﴾, meaning the one whose habit is to *yakhnas*, that is, to hide, withdraw, and delay, and conceal himself after appearing, time after time. Whenever remembrance (*dhikr*) occurs, he retreats, and whenever it ceases, he returns to his whispering. So remembrance for him is like maces that suppress the corrupter. He is intensely repelled by it. For this reason, the devil of the believer is emaciated, as is related from some of the early scholars that the believer drives away his devil as a man drives away his camel on a journey. Al-Baghawi said: "It has a snout like the snout of a dog in the chest of the human. It is said: its head is like the head of a snake, placing its head on the right of the heart, speaking to it. When he remembers Allah, he retreats, and when he does not remember Allah, he returns and places his head." May Allah the Exalted disgrace him.

When he mentioned the attribute of the one from whom refuge is sought, he mentioned his manifesting his attribute through action, so he said: ﴿Who whispers﴾, meaning he casts harmful meanings in a manner of concealment and repetition, such that their concepts reach [the heart] without hearing. He indicated the abundance of his whispering by mentioning the chest (*ṣadr*), which is the courtyard of the heart and its dwelling, so he said: ﴿in the breasts of people﴾, meaning those who are agitated when they are heedless of the remembrance of their Lord, for it is the corridors of the hearts through which incoming things enter into them. This is like the estimative faculty (*al-quwwa al-wahmiyya*): the intellect assists with the true premises that produce a certain conclusion, but when the matter reaches that point, the estimative faculty recoils while the intellect slackens for a little while from the conclusion, so the estimative faculty (p. 434) begins whispering, and the natural disposition accepts from it, by virtue of its affinity with the estimative darkness that it has. And "people" (*al-nās*): al-Qamus says: it applies to humans and jinn; it is the plural of *insān* (human), whose origin is *unās*, the plural of *ʿazīz*, to which the definite article was added. End of quote. Perhaps its application to these two opposites is in view of the *nawas* (swaying), whose root meaning is agitation and oscillation, so it would be a *naḥt* (blend) formed from two roots: *ins* and *nawas*, and a third: *nisyān* (forgetting).

(p. 435) When the one who teaches man evil is sometimes from the jinn and sometimes from mankind, He said, clarifying the whisperer and warning against the devils of mankind just as He warned against the devils of the jinn, giving precedence to the more important and more harmful. It is also permissible that it be an explanation of "mankind," and there is no artificiality in this, as is known from the transmission of the Qamus (the lexicon): ﴿From the jinn﴾, meaning the jinn who are at the utmost extent of evil, rebelliousness and concealment, ﴿and mankind﴾, meaning the people of agitation and wavering, whether they are from mankind or from the jinn. So the meaning is that some of the jinn are empowered over others, just as they are empowered over mankind. Thus the devil of the jinn enters the jinni [just as he enters the human] and whispers to him. This was said by al-Baghawi, quoting al-Kalbi, who said: It was related of some of the Arabs that he said: A group of the jinn came and stood, and it was said: "Who are you?" They said: "People from among the jinn." He said: This is the meaning of the statement of al-Farra'.

The surah has been concluded with what it began with. The second meaning is more fitting for linking its last part to its first, for it becomes an explanation of "mankind," to whom the sublime attributes were ascribed. The thoughts that come to a human being may be a whisper (waswasa), and they may be an inspiration (ilham). Inspiration sometimes comes from God without an intermediary, and sometimes through the intermediary of the angel, and each of the two occurs in the heart. Whisper sometimes comes from the devil and sometimes from the self (nafs), and both occur in the chest. If the person is vigilant, he repels the harm from himself; otherwise the incursions overwhelm him and take firm hold of him. The good of thoughts is distinguished from their evil by the standard of the Shari'a, although the matter is difficult, for the devil strives hard at deception. If [a thought] agrees with the Shari'a, he should consider it: if doing it now is better, without forfeiting another virtue that is superior to it, [he should] hasten to it. If the thought is worldly, and reflection leads to the conclusion that it is beneficial without contravening the Shari'a, he should, in addition to intense contemplation, seek counsel from one whom he trusts in his religion and intellect, and then perform istikhara (prayer for guidance), in case the minds may agree upon it, and in case there is a flaw from a shortcoming that occurred in the consideration. Some have made the criterion of the merciful (rahmani) thought that the chest expands for it and the soul is at peace with it, while the criterion of the satanic and the self-driven [thought] is that the chest contracts at it and the soul is disturbed, based on the testimony of the Prophetic hadith concerning righteousness and sin. The satanic is recognized by its driving toward mere opposition, for the devil has no aim in a specific opposition; if remembrance (dhikr) occurs, that goes away. The self-driven is bound to a specific thing, whether it is benefit or harm, and is not turned away by remembrance. The devil may be a human being among wives, children and acquaintances, and he may sometimes be more harmful than the devil of the jinn, so its remedy is cutting off and avoidance according to ability. Whoever wants a great standard for whom to keep company with and whom to avoid should consult the verse of the Cave:

﴿And restrain yourself to be with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair has been [ever] in loss.﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]

Just as its ending returned to its beginning, so too among the great correspondences is the correspondence of its meaning with al-Fatiha, so that the end of the Qur'an returns to its beginning, and its starting point joins with its returning point in the best manner, as has been explained previously from Surat Quraysh up to here, surah by surah. The relation of this surah to al-Fatiha and its joining with it is from the aspect that al-Fatiha includes three names: Allah, al-Rabb (the Lord) and al-Malik (the King), and by being the Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an) it adds al-Rahman and al-Rahim, because these two include all the blessings, apparent and hidden, which are contained in the attribute of lordship (rububiyya). Surat an-Nas includes al-Rabb, al-Malik and al-Ilah (the God), which is the root of the name of majesty (ism al-jalala). Al-Fatiha is distinguished by the name in which no partnership at all occurs. Since it is established throughout the Qur'an that He is the true God, and that no partner to Him in divinity is valid in any way, just as there is no partnership in the greatest name with which the Qur'an opens, neither in truth nor falsehood, the Noble Qur'an concluded with it, expressing it as "God" for the clarity of the matter and the complete absence of ambiguity. The conclusion has become, from what the opening was with, in the most manifest manner and the first arrangement. The other two names remain in their order. Thus the arrangement becomes, if you join the end of an-Nas to the beginning of al-Fatiha: "Ilah, Malik, Rabb [Allah, Rabb], Rahman, Rahim, Malik," as an announcement that the referent of the greatest name is the true God, and He is the greatest King, because to Him belong creation, the excellence of nurture, and mercy, both general and particular.

The essence of Surat an-Nas is seeking refuge in this described Lord from the whisper of the breast, which produces vigilance (muraqaba), just as the essence of Surat al-Fatiha is the emptying of the secret from preoccupations, which requires confining the aspirations to Him, glorified and exalted be He, and remaining in His lofty presence by restricting permanence to Him and judging the perishing of all else. That is the highest degree of vigilance. So when God, the Truth, wants to assist a servant, He moves him to seek help by seeking refuge, and He facilitates for him sincere reliance (tawakkul). Then he becomes (p. 438) a sincere worshipper in servitude, and his God becomes his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. It is fitting that, whenever He, glorified and exalted be He, brings him closer, he increases in worship for Him, until he is freed from the deception of the devil by death, as He, exalted be He, said to the nearest of His creation to Him, Muhammad ﷺ:

﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]

Whoever diminishes any of the deeds, relying on the fact that he has arrived, has become a heretic (tazandaqa), and his parable is that of a person in a dark house who lit a lamp in it, and it shone, so he said: "I only lit the lamp so that it would illuminate the house, and it has illuminated, so I have no need now for the lamp," and he extinguished it, and the darkness returned as it was.

The Prophet ﷺ urged the beginning of the Qur'an after its completion, as the continuity of the meaning with what I have explained indicates, and that is called the "travelling one who halts" (al-hal al-murtahil). It is as if the reciter, by the command to seek refuge, was reminded of the intention to begin his recitation, so it is as if it was said: "Seek refuge, O one who has completed the Mighty Qur'an, in order to begin it." It is also as if, when he sought refuge by what He commanded in this surah, it was said to him: "Then what will you do?" He said: "I will begin." Or, when He commanded seeking refuge, he said: "What shall I do?" and it was said: "Begin with: In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful," whose vigilance is obligatory at the ends and beginnings of matters, for nothing occurs except by Him. Or the basmala is the object of the saying in "Say" [al-Nas: 1], in the manner of "I seek refuge" [al-Nas: 1], or a substitute for "the Lord of mankind" [al-Nas: 1]. It is as if He commanded seeking protection, and the invocation of the name (tasmiya) is a command to repel and to attract. That is because when He commanded this seeking of protection, and He, glorified be He, had said:

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]

it was known that what is meant is beginning the Qur'an with it. Its relation to al-Fatiha is the relation of the effect to its cause. So it is as if it was said: "Seek refuge by this Greatest Lord, besides whom there is no king and no god, for to Him belongs praise, and He is the encompassing of everything, so He is capable of everything, the subduer of everything in the Hereafter, and He is the refuge and the recourse. There is no god but Him." For the name is the attribute, and what is meant by it is the category, so the meaning of "In the name of Allah" is "by His attribute or by His beautiful attributes." Praise (hamd) is the commendation by a beautiful attribute, so it is as if it was said: "I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind by His beautiful attributes, for to Him belongs praise, which is all the beautiful attributes, for beginning in it requires power, so He has complete power, or knowledge, and knowledge is His attribute, or generosity, and likewise." The conclusion is that it is as if it was said: He is sought as refuge from the devil by the name which none shares with Him, because it comprises all the beautiful names, that is, the attributes free from any deficiency, especially the attribute of general mercy which has enveloped me in its embrace and whose assistance has raised me up; then the particular mercy, of which I am most worthy to seek the rain, because of the deficiency within me that prevents me from it and distances me from it, for whoever follows his fortunes is distanced from it. So I ask Him to make me among its people, and to carry me in both abodes with its connection, so that I may be among the people of His pleasure, so that I worship none but Him.

You may also establish the connection and joining in another way, manifestly complete and of wondrous order, saying: When the meeting of the end of the surah-circle with its beginning drew near, and its last part with its first, and its detail with its connector, the resemblance of the two heads became intense. So these last three surahs became akin to the first three in aims and in the abundance of virtues and benefits: Surat al-Ikhlas (Sincerity) with Surat Al 'Imran, for it is one; and al-Falaq with al-Baqara in correspondence and agreement, for the Book, which is the aim of Surat al-Baqara, is the best of matters, so it is for assistance with the best of matters; and al-Falaq with al-'Awidh (the two refuges) concerning the evil of creation, the one who counts every good. And in al-Baqara:

﴿I seek refuge in Allah that I should be among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqara: 67]

﴿They teach people magic﴾ [al-Baqara: 102], and the verses.

[p. 441] ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from their own selves﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:109] [the verse ends here]. The people (an-nas) correspond to al-Fatihah. When the breast, which is the dwelling of the heart (al-qalb), which is the vehicle of the spirit (ar-ruh), which is the source of the intellect (al-'aql), is emptied, then comes vigilance (al-muraqabah). This amounts to sanctifying the soul through Tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and sincerity (al-ikhlas). Then comes seeking refuge (al-isti'adhah) from every evident evil and from every hidden harm, so that one becomes fit to recite the surah of vigilance, along with what the traveling state calls for and what follows it of the Book, [p. 441 continued] with the utmost soundness and correctness. It seems he first sufficed with the well-known seeking of refuge, just as one suffices, at the beginnings of matters, with the easiest of commands. When he completed the closing, he was rewarded with seeking refuge from the Qur'an, as an elevation to the station of excellence (al-ihsan). Thus the last joined the first, with a connection that admits no doubt, and was united with it in every kind of union. Indeed in that is a reminder for people of understanding. This is what God makes easy to grasp of the meanings of its arrangement and its sentences, in relation to their concepts and causes. There remains the consideration of what the numbers of its words point to, through the subtle hints and allusions of its symbols. Its words number twenty, which correspond, if you count from the beginning of prophethood, to the year of the lesser pilgrimage of the Qada' (the Year of the Qada'), which was the seventh year after the Hijrah, in which the security from what Satan whispered was manifested, [p. 442] in the year of the Hudaybiyyah lesser pilgrimage, concerning the vision of the Prophet ﷺ of entering the House and circling it. If you add to them the three pronouns, they become twenty-three, which corresponds to the tenth year after the Hijrah, the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, which cut off the effect of Satan's whispering that had been at the beginning of the eleventh year, at the death of the Prophet ﷺ, toward the Arabs in the affair of the apostasy (ar-riddah). God protected [the Muslims] from its evil by the resolve of as-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, until he returned the people to the religion and cast down upon them the whisperings of the corrupting devils. [The word of the Muslims was united] in confirmation of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed Satan has despaired that he will be worshipped in the Arabian Peninsula after this day." If you add to them the words of the basmalah, they become twenty-seven, corresponding to the year in which the affair of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab al-Faruq, may God be pleased with him, was firmly established, he who never took a path except that Satan took another path than it. That was in the fourteenth year after the Hijrah. This is with regard to its words. If you consider it from the standpoint of its letters, it has great secrets from another standpoint. Among them: its words together with the words of al-Fatihah are arranged from twenty-six letters, which are all of the nine and twenty letters of the alphabet except the thā' (ث), the zā' (ز), and the ẓā' (ظ) [the text as given], each of the two of which [the surahs] has twenty letters, sharing eighteen of them, and each one of them has four exclusively: al-Fatihah has the unpointed ḥā' and ṭā', and the pointed ḍād and ghayn; and an-Nas has the pointed jīm, khā', and shīn, and the fā'. Ibn Mayleq said: seven letters fell from al-Fatihah: "thaja khaza shathaf" [the text as given]. [p. 443] Perhaps in that, God knows best, there is an indication that the completion of the revelation of the Qur'an from its beginning to its end, in the number of letters that each of the two surahs at its beginning and its end comprises, corresponds to twenty-two years, and the twenty-third year is the arrival at the presence of the Living, the Self-Subsisting, glory be to Him and exalted: how great is His affair, how mighty His dominion, how firm His proof.

Its author, may God have mercy on him, said: This is the completion of what I intended of Nazm ad-Durar (The Arrangement of Pearls) concerning the correspondence of verses and surahs. It is the interpreter of the Qur'an, the one who manifests the correspondences of the Criterion (al-Furqan). It is a tafsir the ages have never heard the like of, nor has any of the many tafsirs overflowed with its abundance as a heavy rain. I finished the draft on Tuesday, the seventh of Sha'ban in the year 875 AH, in my mosque at the Rahbat Bab al-'Id in Cairo the Victorious. My beginning on it was in Sha'ban of the year 861 AH, so that is fourteen full years. I finished this clean copy on Sunday afternoon, the tenth of Sha'ban, in the year 882 AH, in my house adjoining the Badra'iyyah madrasah in Damascus. That is twenty-two years, corresponding to the number of years of the bright, delightful, exalted, pure, blessed, and pure prophethood. Had it not been for God's help, it would have been nonexistent, or incomplete and deficient. After I had gone deep into it and its structures were set straight for me, and I had reached nearly half of it, the learned men praised it highly for the excellence of its composition, the abundance of its meanings, and the firmness of its arrangement [p. 444]. But the disease of envy crept into a group of people of hardship, deceit, and obstinacy, who want leadership by falsehood, and each of them is devoid of the essence of knowledge. The night of ignorance extended its darkness over them, and the dust of foolishness raised its blackness and gloom over their heads. They aimed the arrows of evils, falsehoods, and all kinds of lies. They greatly multiplied disparagement with reproach, ugly abuse, and vile vilification, with error-charging and misguidance, by quoting from the Torah and the Gospel. Therefore upright statements were composed on the ruling regarding quoting from ancient books, in which I explained that this is a straight practice, to support the great Hanif religion. Through this I brought forth the text of ash-Shafi'i, and the words of an-Nawawi and ar-Rafi'i, and I had the noble scholars copy the book, and they wrote what I had deposited in Masa'id an-Nazar li-ash-Shirāf 'ala Maqasid as-Suwar (The Ascents of Reflection for Overlooking the Aims of the Surahs). Then God extinguished their fire, manifested their faults, and exposed their disgrace and shame. Then they persisted in a perpetual innovation, so I composed in it the well-known statement, and explained their opposition to the Book and the Sunnah, their falling into the very sedition, and their breaching of the greatest Paradise, and the explicit text of ash-Shafi'i and the transmissions of the scholars. They became like one who has put a stone in his mouth or whose mouth is filled with water. Then they rose up in the sedition of Ibn al-Farid, all of them being stubborn opponents, [p. 445] and they incited the rabble of people against me, so the rays of might intensified, and they nearly converged into reversal. They aimed at the path of heresy and exaggerated in elevating [some] from the people of incarnation (al-ittihad). They persisted in contention with obstinacy, issued verdicts purely of falsehood, and spread deadly poison, except for a few people, whom God guaranteed with victory despite their weakness. I asked them a question which made them astray and ignorant. They passed it around among themselves and transmitted it, and they were unable to answer it after striving with the utmost effort, and they tried it, so their state became evident to most people, their misguidance became famous among them, and their clear error and absurdity. I composed on this several works in which their disgraceful deeds became apparent and their hidden things were exposed. Among them: Sawab al-Jawab li-as-Sa'il al-Murtab (The Correct Answer to the Doubting Questioner); among them: al-Qarid li-Takfir Ibn al-Farid (The Vein-Cutter for the Takfir of Ibn al-Farid); among them: Tadmir al-Mu'arid fi Takfir Ibn al-Farid (The Destruction of the Opponent in the Takfir of Ibn al-Farid); among them: Tanbih al-Ghabi 'ala Takfir Ibn 'Arabi (Alerting the Dull to the Takfir of Ibn 'Arabi); among them: Tahdhir al-'Ibad min Ahl al-'Inad bi-Bid'at al-Ittihad (Warning the Servants against the Obstinate People with the Innovation of Incarnation). I spent a long life on them, and they wasted my time, may God waste them utterly, and may He threaten their pillars and supports with a threat. I humbled them with the inability to answer, which revealed doubt, morning and evening, repeatedly and openly. Then the rebuke, reproach, and condemnation compelled them to write an answer, which was not free from confusion and instability, doubt [p. 446] and hesitation. I made clear that its compiler erred in all of its correctness, that he disbelieved explicitly in four places, and lied in eight, so he became wounded, indeed a fallen corpse. I extended that rebuke, reproach, and condemnation, so their necks were humbled, their opposition weakened, and their hypocrisy hidden. Yet in each of these events there occurred, from evils and wondrous decrees, what its darkness covered over, rising like suns.

The matter dragged on for years, distress spread until much groaning arose, and supplication and longing in prayer. God gave steadfastness and granted patience and forbearance until I completed this book, in the form you see of beauty and correctness.

I have said, praising the aforementioned book, showing through it the wondrous decrees and strange affairs, explaining my situation and theirs, the attainment of my hopes and the frustration of their hopes, in mujazu' ar-rajaz meter, its rhythmic ending is cut, the rhyme is continuous, absolute, and unadorned, naming it "Kitab Lamma" (The Book of "Lamma"), because the main purpose is to show the connection of sentences to one another, such that each sentence holds fast to what precedes it and is joined to it. That is the intended manifest aspect of speech, its secret and core, which is for speech like the spirit, while explaining the meanings of individual words is like the body, each sentence on its own. The spirit is the greatest aim, which is grasped by one who tastes and understands, whose mind travels through the fields of structures and knows. "Lamma" is a temporal adverb used to indicate the occurrence of the second of what it governs upon the occurrence of the first, with the greatest possibility, meaning that it is like conditionals that require two clauses such that the one implies the other. The book is completed in this arrangement with "Lamma," because I greatly used it in it for this purpose:

Here is the Book of "Lamma," which gathered meanings with full gathering,
whose seas of knowledge flow with abundant flowing.
I gave good tidings to whoever envies it that he will die of grief,
for my intention is sound, and I strove in it with resolve.
Our Lord accepts it in quality and quantity,
and by what I intended, He has encompassed it in knowledge.
I endured from my envious ones for a time what was grievous,
they counted years, giving my heart the poison of the grave.
How many times they humiliated me, and how many times they shot me with arrows,
they pressed my heart with harm and extended their blame.
How many times they lay in wait for my slip, yet they found no crime in me,
and they weakened my seekers' murmur and resolve.
They threatened them with harm and weakened their stoning,
I cast harm when Blaze intensified, when harm was intended for stoning.
I cast when the night darkened and calamity made it dark,
their harm and injustice, by a call into darkness.
I call upon God against them, saying: "O Allah!"
O my Lord, I am striving, so relieve my grief, O my God.
I have no sin with them except the Book of "Lamma."
The springs of guidance flowed from it, and it became a sea.
I composed it while in the seas of its knowledge is what surged,
and it has risen in structure and become sweet in arrangement.
I made it as counsel for one who loves knowledge,
I deposited in it pearls at which the understanding dances.
They bring sight out of blindness by its gentleness, and make the deaf hear,
its precious knowledge is specific, and for humans it is general.
It makes speak whoever sings with it, even if they were mute,
its deeds are glorious, I seek refuge for them in the Names.
My Lord made its matter easy for me until it was completed,
in fourteen years, silent [in counting, as in the text].
The tongue of counting said: "Take to you a full moon,"
and no one diminishes an incomplete one, O my companion, in a day.
I seek refuge for it in the Chosen One from the evil of a blameworthy wretch,
and from an envier who has become anxious because of it.
So none seeks its blame except one hated, most blind.
My Lord sufficed me against their evil and adorned its names,
and returned their scheming to their own destruction and loss,
and returned them in their rage, since they did not attain a boy,
and increased it in happiness, and blessings clung to it.

Thus spoke the one who humbly stands before the Creator in need of the Creator's pardon, Abu al-Hasan Ibrahim ibn 'Umar ibn Hasan ar-Ribat ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Bakr al-Biqa'i ash-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, saying: "All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds, and may God send blessings upon our master Muhammad, his family, and his companions, and grant them abundant peace, always and forever, until the Day of Religion. God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 114, verse 6 (part 3 of 3):

The completion of this part was by the hand of the least of Allah's servants and the one most in need of Allah's gentleness and pardon, ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥawwilī al-Shāfiʿī, resident of the sacred city of Allah, may Allah forgive him, his parents, his teachers, and all Muslims, in the blessed city of Makkah the Honoured, on Saturday, the blessed twenty-sixth of the auspicious month of Ṣafar, in the year 944 AH. My age has now passed seventy-five years. I ask Allah for a good end, steadfastness upon the religion of Islam, and death in one of His two sanctuaries, by His bounty. May Allah send blessings and abundant peace upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), his family and companions, always and forever until the Day of Religion. Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

There is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

Some of the author's students, al-ʿArs Khalīl ibn Mūsā al-Muqriʾ, said in praise of the aforementioned book called Lammā:

Proof of the religion [of Allah] has become one who clarifies the secrets of the word of Allah in the Qur'an.
And he has brought what the people left behind after him, walking behind it forever through the ages.
So whoever claims to weave a pattern like his has claimed what is not within possibility.
And if the exegete one day seeks to come with its like, he comes without acquiescence.
We said to him: explain, and compare after this, and for us is the proof against you, with clear evidence.

The completion of copying this second half of the book called Lammā, Munāsabāt al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm (the connections between the surahs and verses of the Great Qur'an), upon the one to whom the best prayers and peace were sent, was on the thirteenth night of the month of Jumādā al-Ūlā in the year 997 AH, by the hand of the most worthless of servants and the one most in need of the forgiveness of his Generous Lord, Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Badrashīnī by town, Shāfiʿī by school of law, praying and sending peace upon the best, most perfect, and most beautiful of Allah's creation, Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and upon his family, companions, wives, descendants, and the people of his household, the good and pure, with blessings and peace that are lasting and continuous for as long as Allah's dominion endures. There is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty. Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs. Amen, amen.

If you encounter a fault, do not hasten to revile me,
for I am a man not free from slips.
